subject: blueprintSpitfire
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Spitfire fighter plane.
Style: cyanotype blueprint.

spec.name: Spitfire Blueprint
spec.description: A Supermarine Spitfire Mk I fighter drawn as a cyanotype blueprint: deep Prussian-blue airframe with white-line panel seams, ribs, rivets and callout details, standing on its undercarriage.
spec.layout: Single-engine low-wing monoplane facing +Z. Propeller spinner at z=+4.2, long nose with Merlin cowl, cockpit with bubble canopy at z~0 to -0.9, tapering fuselage to a tail at z=-4.4 with fin and tailplane. Elliptical wings span x=+-5.6 at y~1.0, with a slight dihedral, round tips, and the gear legs under the wing at x=+-1.4. Tail wheel under the rear. Everything is a flat cyanotype colour: Prussian-blue hull panels, paler cyan wing skin, and white linework as thin parts (panel seams, ribs, rivet rows, roundel rings, stencil bars) seated on surfaces. Lowest points (tyres) rest on y=0. Roundels are concentric flat discs: white, mid blue, pale cyan.

parts.builds: Engine nose forward of z=0.8: Merlin cowling loft in hullBlue, exhaust stacks (3 per side as small deepBlue cylinders with line rings), cowl panel seams and rivet rows in line, spinner cone in deepBlue with a line band, the three-blade propeller on the propeller joint (prop blue, white tip stripes), radiator scoop under the nose.
parts.attaches: Meets fuselage at z=0.8 on the body joint; prop on propeller joint at spinnerBase.

parts.builds: Fuselage from z=0.8 to the tail root at z=-4.4: lofted tapering hullBlue body with paleCyan belly sector, white seam rings and a longitudinal seam, rivet rows, the glass bubble canopy with line frame ribs and sliding rail, headrest, gun-sight, fuselage roundels on both sides (white, blue, cyan discs), serial stencil bars, a cockpit interior in deepBlue with stick and seat.
parts.attaches: Front at nose z=0.8; wings at wingRoot; tail at tailRoot.

parts.builds: Two elliptical wings from the wingRoot, in wingBlue top and paleCyan underside, sweeping to rounded tips at x=+-5.6, slight dihedral, thickness tapering. Detail as separate parts: rib lines in white spanwise and chordwise, aileron and flap hinge lines, four-gun port panels with small barrels, wing roundels on the top surface, landing light, rivet rows, a white outline along the leading edge, and wing-root fillets.
parts.attaches: Root at wingRoot on the body joint; gear legs hang from the gearL and gearR mounts.

parts.builds: Empennage at the rear: vertical fin and rudder as extrudes in hullBlue with white hinge line and ribs and a roundel flash, horizontal tailplanes with elevators (elliptical, span x=+-1.6), tail cone, a tailwheel leg and small tyre on the tailWheel joint, an arrestor hook, a navigation light, and rivet and rib lines.
parts.attaches: Root at tailRoot on the body joint; tailwheel on the tailWheel joint.

parts.builds: Main undercarriage: two oleo legs in metal on the gearL/gearR joints splayed outward, with a white torque link, a fork, a tyre (tyre colour, 12 sides) and hub disc with line spokes, plus wheel-well door panels in deepBlue hung beside each leg, brake line details and cyan highlight rings. Tyre bottoms at y=0.
parts.attaches: Hangs from the gearL and gearR mounts under the wings.

I'm planning the buildGear function signature and setting up a safe color accessor that pulls from the palette object with fallback defaults for hull, wing, glass, tyre, and metal tones.

For the geometry, I'm sketching out the landing gear design with splayed oleo legs running from the joint near the wing root down and outward to wheel hubs, calculating positions so the tyres sit flush at ground level and fit within the fuselage's bounding box, then mirroring the whole assembly across both sides using the gearL/gearR joint naming convention.

I'm now working out the leg strut itself as two cylinder segments of different thickness, and deciding the wheel fork should be single-sided on the inboard side rather than a symmetric double prong, matching a typical Spitfire-style gear layout.

Still working out the leg-to-fork-to-axle geometry, then setting up the tire as a short cylinder rotated along the x-axis to represent the wheel.

Adding wheel detail layers...

I'm also adding rim and sidewall highlight rings, plus the scissor-style torque link arms connecting points along the leg with a pivot offset forward in z, forming the characteristic V shape.

Now I'm thinking through leg fairing details—adding a flat plate for the gear door, modeled as a thin panel parallel to the leg and hinged inboard, similar to the Spitfire's wheel-well door design.

Still working out door geometry...

I'm positioning the door beside the leg with proper thickness and z-range so it sits within the box bounds, hinged at the top. For details I'm planning a thin hinge rod, rib lines, and a rivet row, trying to keep the part budget around 55 pieces per side by merging the rivets into fewer parts.

I'm working out the local coordinate axes for the door faces, since the cross product of x and y directions determines which way the outer face normal points for each mirrored side — I'm checking whether local z maps to +x or -x for the s=1 and s=-1 cases so the surface details land on the correct outward-facing side.

Rather than fight the local transform, I'm just computing detail placement directly in world coordinates: defining the door's lean plane explicitly with a normalized y-direction vector to avoid a slight scale mismatch, then deriving world positions from that.

With this, I'm placing rods and parts using explicit world coordinates tied to the gear-left bone where appropriate, and planning a brake line as a thin swept path running from the leg down through the fork to the wheel hub.

Now I'm working out the oleo leg itself: upper metal cylinder, a collar ring disc, a lower chrome piston, scissor links, and a top mounting block attaching the leg to the wing.

Adding leg rings and fork pieces...

Checking the clearance confirms the fork stays inboard with a small gap, so I'm adding a brake drum disc overlapping slightly into the tyre and sizing the hub disc to protrude just past the wheel center, keeping the dark tyre sidewall proportions consistent.

Now I'm layering the outer hub detail: a metal disc, a pale cyan ring torus just outside it, and a set of spoke boxes radiating from the hub — working out how many spokes to use so they divide evenly around the wheel.

Adding spokes and tread grooves...

Accepting that ambiguity for now, I'll move to adding rim bolts as small spheres positioned around the hub ring using trig to place them at angle intervals. Then I'm planning the door panel as an extruded shape in deep blue with line details, plus considering adding a leg fairing plate to cover part of the landing gear leg like on the actual Spitfire.

Adjusting fairing proportions...

I'll confirm the sweep accepts `up` for path sources and leave the shift as is. Skipping the wheel-well detail, I'm adding a retraction jack strut from the wing point to the leg, and setting up color fallbacks so hull color defaults gracefully if a named palette entry is missing. I'm also planning a gearWheelL joint nested under gearL to let the wheel spin independently.

I'm now wiring up that wheel joint with the right direction and parent, then moving on to the two-part torque link with its pivot and the scissor-style lower leg geometry, computing leg points by interpolating between the foot and top with a forward offset. Finally I'm setting up a door rivet helper to place fasteners along the door rows.

Thinking through which faces of the door should carry detail lines and rivets, I'm weighing outboard versus inboard visibility given the leg and wheel partially obscure things, and deciding to duplicate the border lines and rivets across both faces while keeping an eye on the growing part budget.

Now I'm tallying up piece counts per component: the leg assembly with its rod, piston, collar, tori rings, plate, fairing, strut and link arms comes to roughly 13 parts; the fork with boss, prongs, axle and nut adds about 4; the wheel with tyre grooves, sidewalls, hub, spokes, bolts and drum rings totals around 25; and I'm starting to break down the door into its panel, hinge rod, and border rod components.

My running total is landing near 134, a bit over the 130 target, so I'm trimming back — reducing rivet counts per face, cutting a tread groove, and simplifying the bolt count to bring the overall tally down closer to 124 while deciding which face should carry the visible rivets.

Defining the door's border outline and panel geometry...

Still working out the door geometry...

Still plotting brake line geometry...

Defining the fairing sweep path and top plate placement...

I'm working on the buildNose function, and since I'm unsure of the exact palette key names, I'm adding a defensive helper that tries a few likely keys with fallback literal colors to stay safe.

Now I'm sketching the geometry: nose span from z=0.8 to 4.3, cowl centered at y=1.5 tapering toward the spinner tip at z=4.2, and propeller radius constrained to about 0.9 by the bounding box, which is smaller than a real Spitfire's prop diameter but fits the constraints given. I'm deciding whether to build the cowling using a loft through stations or a lathe revolve around the z-axis, leaning toward lathe for the cowl outline since the loft API's cross-section shape is uncertain.

For seams, I'll compute them analytically as rings using the surface and loop helpers, cutting a plane through a point facing a direction to get a closed path, then sweeping a thin tube along it for the seam line. For rivet rows, I'll use the along helper to place small sphere parts at even intervals along that same loop, attaching each to a frame.

To keep part counts manageable, I'm planning to merge all the rivet spheres across rings into a single geometry per color using mergeGeometries from BufferGeometryUtils, translating each sphere instance into position rather than creating hundreds of separate parts.

For the body surface, I'm building the cowl as a loft, then running longitudinal seam tubes along it using angle-based lines at the top centerline and at symmetric angles around the circumference, with small lift so they sit just above the surface.

Now I'm working out cowl cross-section dimensions station by station — center y shifting slightly forward to back, widths and heights tapering from about 1.15 near z=0.8 down to roughly 0.78–0.8 by z=2.9, keeping the box roughly symmetric around y≈1.5 to fit the radiator scoop and prop clearances underneath.

I'm also thinking about how the loft's rounded end caps interact with the spinner: at the front (z=3.3), a cap bulge would get hidden inside the spinner base (radius 0.4), which is fine, but at the rear (z=0.8) a round cap could awkwardly bulge into the fuselage, so I need to handle that transition carefully.

I decide to go with flat caps for the loft, uncertain whether that option is actually supported, but proceeding anyway. For the spinner itself, I'm setting up a lathe shape along the z-axis at the propeller joint, defining a tapered outline from base to tip, with 12 segments, attached to the propeller bone, and colored deep blue — then adding a thin lathe ring band nearby.

Interpolating the spinner's radius profile to figure out exactly where the band sits...

Setting up the propeller blades now — three blades extruded from a 2D outline, oriented radially around the hub using radial and tangential direction vectors per blade angle, with thickness along the cross product axis.

I'm placing the blade near the spinner so it emerges from the slot at z≈3.45, keeping the start radius small so it's partially hidden by the spinner body. I'm considering adding pitch twist by tilting the tangential axis slightly but deciding it may be unnecessary complexity to skip for now.

Still writing blade geometry...

I'm deciding on two white stripe bands near the tip with an edge-interpolation helper to fit the blade outline, then settling on a deep blue color for the prop blade against the hull/spinner tones.

Now I'm adding a small metal cuff at the blade root, then placing three exhaust stacks per side on the cowl, angled backward and positioned along the upper sides using surface-hit geometry to align them correctly.

Adding end detailing to each stack—a torus ring at the tip, a dark tire-colored disc for the opening, and a slightly larger mid ring—bringing each stack to 4 parts, roughly 24 total across all six stacks.

Still working out the plate geometry...

Now I'm mapping out the cowl panel seams—rings at several z heights plus longitudinal lines, and a lip ring near the front using a torus for the circular edge detail, sized to match the cowl's width and height profile.

For the top of the cowl, I want to add the characteristic Spitfire hump fairing, plus small rocker cover bumps on either side representing the cylinder heads, placed as elongated flat boxes angled outward along the engine cowling.

I'll tilt the long box slightly to follow the cowl slope, orienting it with the surface normal and embedding it enough to hide the ends cleanly. For the chin intake under the nose, I'm planning a small lofted scoop shape positioned under the cowl rather than the wing radiators, since the spec calls for a nose-mounted intake.

Adding the scoop opening as a dark recessed box with a thin rim built from small bars outlining the intake at the nose...

Adding rivet details and fasteners along the cowl rings, using small merged sphere geometries positioned at intervals around each seam to simulate dzus fasteners and panel rivets.

So angle 90 lands on the right side, and I want symmetric longitudinal seams straddling the exhaust plate near azimuth 90/elevation 15, using an explicit center point so directions stay purely lateral. I'm also setting up a paleCyan lower belly sector using loft with a color option.

Actually, to reduce risk I'll switch to a sweep with an explicit path and radius function instead of loft, since that's more clearly documented — using a catmull path through station centers and interpolating radii by z-fraction as a stand-in for arc-length t, with the cowl line feeding into the same sweep call.

For the cowl I'll bump circle sides up to 16 for smoother facets while keeping flat caps, and use the same bone-anchored sweep approach for the scoop with a box section and a radius function returning half-width/half-height. I'm mapping the z-range of the cowl stations into a normalized t and piecing together a linear interpolation across the station knots to drive the radius function.

Defining station radii/centers...

Then I'll widen the cowl at 0.8 to rx .62, ry .58 to better fit the fuselage width. The surface queries pull from the sweep mesh in model space, which is fine, and the prop shaft/hub plus a small white spinner-tip ring are handled. For joint assignments, I'm using J.body for the cowl and J.propeller for the spinner, blades, and bands/stripes -- no extra joint needed. For blueprint detailing I'll skip the "Merlin" stencil idea and instead add small tick-mark callouts and a stencil row of tiny boxes on the left cowl side panel.

I'm sketching out a rough part budget: cowl stencil bars as small line boxes mirrored on both sides (12 parts total), then tallying up the rest -- cowl meshes, seam rings and longitudinals, rivets, lip torus, spinner, bands, backplate, blades, stripes, cuffs, exhaust stacks, plates, rocker covers, scoop, and the opening rim -- to keep the overall part count within a reasonable budget.

I'm considering adding a small inspection hatch outline on each side as four thin boxes forming a rectangle, and thinking through a helper function that would place these bars using a frame-relative "moved" point so they align properly with the fuselage's local axes.

Defining the hatch bar geometry, using separate flow directions for forward versus vertical bars to orient each stick correctly along the surface.

I'm placing hatches at specific heights and elevations with small fastener details, estimating the total part count stays within budget, then setting up a mirror loop across both sides using symmetric azimuth offsets.

Now I'm starting the actual implementation: importing Three.js utilities, skipping the unused rng import, and setting up a color palette helper that pulls from the provided colors with fallbacks before defining the nose-building function.

Defining cowl profile points...

I'm finishing the interpolation helper, then using it to find ring centers along the z-axis for seam loops. For each ring, I'm extracting a loop from the surface and sweeping a thin diamond-cross-section rope along it to mark the seam lines, checking that the closed-path sweep with a bone reference behaves correctly.

I'm setting the tube sides to 4 for a flattened, line-like rope appearance, then planning rivet rows at specific z positions with alternating offsets, collecting sample points along each rivet path to later place small spheres at those locations.

Still writing rivet placement logic...

I'm also sketching out longitudinal cowl lines at a few angles to add surface detail.

I'm reworking the seam and hatch placement so the lines at 0, ±40, and ±130 avoid overlapping the plate region (62–88°) and the hatch marks near elevation −22, shifting the hatch clock position so it clears the boundary seam at 130 cleanly.

Now I'm adding stacks at elevation 20, checking plate width (clock 58–82) stays clear of the ±40 line, then for each z position tracing a surface hit, computing the outward normal blended with a backward direction, and placing a short rod from the surface point out to a tip to build the stack geometry.

Now I'm adding a plate along the cowl's z-axis, checking how the surface curvature affects whether the plate's ends sit flush or hover above the tapering surface near the front.

Thinking about stencil bars for the plate—considering placing small line marks along the plate's surface using positioned sticks offset from the plate's hit frame.

I should create a generic `put(geo, color, point, normal, flow?, embed?)` helper that builds a frame from a point and direction and sticks geometry onto the body bone — this keeps the bone binding intact while letting me position things anywhere. I'll reuse this for the hatch bars too, computing their position from the hit point offset by forward/up vectors and orienting along the surface normal.

Now I realize the stencil bars on the plates need more care since the plate surface is tilted by the slope — just offsetting along world forward introduces error (up to 0.045 at the extremes). Instead I'll project the forward vector onto the plate's tangent plane (removing the component along the normal), normalize that, and use it to place points accurately on the plate surface; I'll wrap this as a `tang(hit)` helper and reuse it for the hatch bars as well.

I'll apply the same per-bar nearest-surface query for hatch marks so they stick properly to the curved surface with embed 0.5. The stencil bars sit on the flat plate geometry separately since the plate isn't part of the cowl surface, while rocker covers get their own ray-cast placement with deep embedding and a possible smaller rim box on top for detail.

Adding bolt rivets along the covers...

Adding lathe band details...

Now I'm figuring out the propeller blade cuffs and roots - small cylinders positioned radially just outside the spinner surface, sized and angled to sit flush against the tapering spinner radius, then placing blades at 120-degree intervals starting from straight up.

Defining blade outline points...

Adding the stripe geometry now, computing inset trapezoid shapes between the lower and upper edge curves for the white accent bands near the tip, with a thin extrusion thickness placed on the same frame as the blade.

I'm also deciding against adding a root ridge line or chord line on the blade—skipping those details—and shifting focus to building the scoop geometry, mapping out sweep path stations along z from 1.2 to 2.5 with center points tracking the cowl bottom position.

For the scoop's cross-section, I'm defining a tapering half-width and half-height function that grows with distance along the path, keeping flat end caps and a boxy section profile. For color, I'm settling on using the hull material for the scoop body with a darker tone for the opening to make it read clearly against the pale cyan cowl belly.

Now I'm placing the rim geometry at the open end of the scoop: a flat rectangular opening centered at the scoop's terminus, with thin frame bars along the top, bottom, and sides, plus a few vertical grille bars spaced across the opening width to suggest intake detailing.

Adding rivet rows at specific seam heights with counts like 24, skipping the cooling gills and oil cooler details, and deciding against blueprint dimension callouts since this is just the airframe part. Now I'm setting up the hit/put helper vectors and the frame function before writing the hatch function.

Working out the hatch orientation logic...

Placing stencil text and hatch markings at specific elevations and heights, then laying out the plate bars as a series with varying lengths and consistent width/height, each attached via frame sticks with vertical flow direction.

I'm working through how the embed fraction offsets the box geometry relative to the surface -- figuring out whether the part's origin sits at the surface or whether the embed value shifts the base below it by embed times height.

Then I'm computing matching placement rules for bars and plates along the flow tangent, confirming the offset formula holds consistently for plate hits, and tracing how stack positions derive from hits along the plate's z-range.

I'm deciding to skip extra details like soot streaks and cowl troughs to keep things manageable, settling on 24 total stacks across the layout, and adding a simple dimmed ring detail to the spinner base before moving into writing the geometry calls for the circular stick parts.

Now I'm finalizing the rivet and loop callbacks for the belly surface sweeps, computing the cowl's lerp parameter from the z-position fraction, and preparing to write out the complete code carefully.

I'm working out the buildTail function, being defensive about ambiguous palette property names by adding a fallback helper that checks multiple possible keys before defaulting. I'm also deciding to avoid importing the Ctx type directly and instead define my own local type for it.

Now I'm designing the actual geometry: a tail cone sweeping from the fuselage's rear joint down to a small radius near z=-4.5, then planning the fin outline by setting up root coordinates for the fin's leading edge and figuring out how to extrude it in profile view.

Sketching the fin's outline points—leading edge curve, rounded top, trailing rudder edge—tapering the thickness toward the root and tip to embed cleanly into the fuselage.

Defining fin and rudder outline coordinates...

Placing the hinge line box, rudder rib lines, and fin ribs with specific positions, then adding the fin flash stripes (the red/white/blue Spitfire tail marking) as thin vertical boxes.

Adjusting stripe box depth...

Now I'm working out the thickness profile from the lowest to highest point of the outline, then turning to the tailplanes: positioning them elliptically around y≈1.72 near the fuselage, figuring out the root chord span in z, and setting up the extrusion axes for the plan-view outline.

I'm reconsidering the layout, deciding to make the fixed tailplane and elevators each a single extrusion spanning the full width, with an elliptical-ish outline—straighter leading edge sweep and curved trailing edge, Spitfire-style. Defining the forward leading-edge curve for the tailplane using a half-ellipse profile across the span.

Now I need to split the ellipse at the hinge line to separate the fixed tail from the elevator. I'm parametrizing the ellipse with v = 0.5(1 - cosφ), solving for the hinge angle φh where v equals 0.62, then using that to define the front (fixed) piece spanning from -φh to φh.

For the elevator, I'll sweep φ the other way through the trailing edge back to the hinge, using roughly 10 points for the front piece and 8 for the elevator -- keeping it simple since the Spitfire's horn-balance detail isn't necessary here. I'll color the elevator with wingBlue and the fixed tailplane with the hull color.

Now working out thickness tapering: tailplane goes from 0.08 at the leading edge to 0.04 at the trailing edge, elevator from 0.045 to 0.02, derived from the outline's v-coordinate range. With the thickness axis pointing up and centered around the fuselage's y-position, I'm adding spanwise rib lines on the top surface as thin raised boxes, computing their chord length at each x position from the leading-edge v-coordinate formula.

Adding hinge marking...

Now I'm working out the elevator ribs — chordwise lines across the elevator surface with thickness tapering from 0.045 near the hinge to 0.02 at the trailing edge, interpolated against v position.

For the rivet rows and ribs, I'm thinking about staying under the 150-part budget by merging geometries via BufferGeometryUtils instead of creating many individual parts, grouping rivets and ribs per bone/colour into single merged meshes.

I'm planning a batch helper per colour that accumulates box/cylinder/sphere geometries with matrix transforms, then flushes them as one merged part at the end—keeping all primitives indexed with consistent position/normal/uv attributes so they merge cleanly, and using the same approach for roundel stripes on the fin.

For the tail cone, I'm checking the taper radii against the fuselage's own end so mine stays slightly smaller and nests inside it, matching the hull colour, and considering shaping it as an ellipse since the Spitfire fuselage is taller than it is wide at the tail.

I also want to add a small glowing nav light sphere at the tail tip using the glow kit, colored pale cyan, positioned at the rear end near the fin base, and I'm working out the joint positions so the fin, body, and tail cone line up correctly along the centreline.

I'll skip the dorsal fillet for now—too fiddly to get right cheaply—and move on to the tailwheel, planning a strut joint at the tail that angles downward to the wheel.

I'm running into a gap though: the fuselage underside near the tail sits around y≈1.55-1.6, but my planned strut/joint heights (0.7, 0.4, 0.78) sit well below that, so I need to reconcile the mount point with the actual fuselage bottom before placing the wheel geometry.

I realize the strut length seems disproportionate for the plane's scale, so I'm considering adding a ventral fairing beneath the tail cone instead—a tapered keel-like shape in hull color running from the tail down toward the wheel mount, similar to what some real aircraft use.

Working out the tailwheel geometry now - placing the strut and fork near the keel's bottom edge around z=-3.95, with the wheel hub trailing slightly behind for a castoring effect.

I'm sizing the tyre cylinder to make sure its bottom edge sits flush with the ground, bumping the segment count to 12 to avoid a visible gap from the polygon apothem.

That gives a bottom vertex exactly at the wheel center minus radius, so rotating the part 90 degrees around Z works cleanly. Now I'm figuring out the arrestor hook placement under the rear fuselage, sketching a rod angled back and down from the keel near the tail with a small hook tip at the end.

I'm noting that glow effects require unpainted parts, so I'll keep that in mind for color handling, and then moving on to add rib and leading-edge trim details to the fin and rudder.

Writing sweep geometry for the leading edge tube, using offset outline points and smooth catmull interpolation to avoid rigid corner splits...

Now I'm budgeting the rivet detail: planning rows of small spheres or low-poly cylinders along the hinge line and ribs, keeping triangle counts low by choosing 5x3 spheres or 6-sided cylinders instead of denser shapes to stay under the 12,000 triangle budget.

I'm also considering whether the tailplane needs a paleCyan underside like the wings and fuselage belly, but deciding that a second extrude layer might be overkill and leaning toward keeping the tailplane as a simpler single-core shape instead.

Now I'm working out the leading edge curve for the fin and planning the classic three-stripe flash decal (white, blue, cyan) near the front, figuring out its box dimensions and position along the fin.

Mapping the fin's local coordinates to world space using the placement origin, then tallying up all the part calls—fin, rudder, tailplane, elevator, keel, cone, strut, fork, tyre, hub, hook, lights—roughly 30 parts total, organized into color batches like line white, dim line, wing blue, pale cyan stripe, and deep blue.

Deciding ring placements along the fuselage/tail junction and setting up a color-lookup helper with fallback keys for hull color. Now I'm planning rib lines on the tail plane at specific chordwise x-positions.
